p.seg: The morning should not be neglected,
nor should the evening be neglected.
When the guest departs,
the host bows to see them off,
and the ceremonial propriety is completely fulfilled.
This shows they know how to be peaceful in feasts without becoming disordered.
46.12 The distinction between noble and base is clear,
the distinctions between prominence and reduction are distinguished,
harmony and joy are achieved without excess,
younger and older brothers are treated without favoritism,
peace and conviviality prevail without chaos.
These five practices
are sufficient to rectify the individual and secure the state.
When that state is secure, the world is secure.
Therefore, it is said:
"I observe these practices in the village,
and know that the way of kings is easy, easy."
46.13 The meaning of the village drinking ceremony is this:
establishing the guest (bīn) to symbolize Heaven,
establishing the host (zhǔ) to symbolize Earth,
setting up the assistant (jiè) and attendant (zhuàn) to symbolize the sun and moon,
and establishing three guests (bīn) to symbolize the three luminaries (sun, moon, and stars).
The ancient system of rites
was based on Heaven and Earth,
governed by the sun and moon,
and guided by the three luminaries.
This is the foundation of governance and education.
46.14 Offering a dog sacrifice in the east
honors the rising of the *yáng* energy in the east.
Washing the sacrificial vessel in the east (zuò),
with the water on the east side of the washing vessel,
honors the left sea of Heaven and Earth.
Honoring the dark liquor (xuán jiǔ)
teaches the people not to forget their roots.
46.15 The guest (bīn) must face south.
The east represents spring,
and the meaning of spring (chūn) is stirring (chǔn),
for the one who produces all things is sagely.
The south represents summer,
and the meaning of summer (xià) is "to nourish" (jiǎ),
nourishing them, growing them, and providing for them;
this is benevolence.
The west represents autumn,
and the meaning of autumn (qiū) is sorrow (chóu);
to be concerned according to the season
They uphold righteousness.
The north represents winter.
Winter, in its meaning, signifies "center".
"Center" means storage.
Therefore, when the Son of Heaven establishes himself,
he positions sagacity and benevolence on the left,
and righteousness and storage on the right.
The armor bearer must face east,
for the armor bearer is the guest of the host.
The host must reside in the east,
for the east represents spring.
Spring, in its meaning, signifies "stirring".
It is that which produces the myriad things.
The host is the one who creates them,
who produces the myriad things.
The moon takes three days to form its first phase,
and three months to complete a season.
Therefore, ritual involves three instances of yielding,
and establishing a state requires appointing three high ministers.
These three guests
are the foundation of governance and education,
and are the great assistants of ritual.
The Meaning of Archery
47.1 In ancient times, when the feudal lords engaged in archery,
they would first perform the Yàn Lǐ (燕禮, Banquet Ritual);
when the qing (卿, high ministers), dàfū (大夫, grand masters),
and shì (士, gentlemen) engaged in archery,
It is necessary to first perform the Xiāng Yǐn Jiǔ zhī Lǐ (鄉飲酒之禮, Village Drinking Rite).
Therefore, the Yàn Lǐ (燕禮, Banquet Rite)
is for clarifying the righteousness between ruler and minister;
the Xiāng Yǐn Jiǔ zhī Lǐ (鄉飲酒之禮, Village Drinking Rite)
is for clarifying the order between elders and juniors.
47.2 Therefore, in archery,
advancing and retreating, circling around must conform to the rites,
the inner intention must be upright,
the outer posture must be straight,
and then one can hold the bow and arrow firmly and securely.
Holding the bow and arrow firmly and securely,
then one can speak of hitting the target.
From this, one can observe virtue and conduct.
47.3 The musical accompaniment:
the Son of Heaven uses "Zōu Yú" (騶虞) as the accompaniment;
the feudal lords use "Lí Shǒu" (貍首) as the accompaniment;
the high officials (Qīng Dàfū, 卿大夫) use "Cǎi Pín" (采蘋) as the accompaniment;
the scholars use "Cǎi Fán" (采繁) as the accompaniment.
"Zōu Yú" (騶虞)
means the music officials are all present;
"Lí Shǒu" (貍首)
means the music meets the proper time;
"Cǎi Pín" (采蘋)
means the music follows the rules;
"Cǎi Fán" (采繁)
means the music does not neglect its duties.
Therefore, the Son of Heaven uses the completeness of officials as the standard;
the feudal lords use timely audience with the Son of Heaven as the standard;
Qīng dàfū regard adherence to the law as moral integrity;
shì regard not losing their position as moral integrity.
Therefore, understanding the aspiration of moral integrity
so as not to fail in one's duty,
then accomplishments will be achieved and virtuous conduct established.
With virtuous conduct established, there will be no disasters of violence and rebellion.
When accomplishments are achieved, the state will be secure.
Therefore, it is said:
"Archery
is a means of observing abundant virtue."
47.4 Therefore, in ancient times, the Son of Heaven selected feudal lords, q卿, dàfū 大夫, and shì 士 through archery.
Archery
is a matter for men,
and thus it is embellished with ritual and music.
Among matters that are performed with utmost ritual and music,
and can be quantified,
to establish virtuous conduct,
nothing is better than archery.
Therefore, the sage kings devoted themselves to it.
47.5 Therefore, the system of the Son of Heaven in ancient times was:
The feudal lords annually presented tribute scholars to the Son of Heaven,
and the Son of Heaven tested them in the archery palace.
Those whose deportment conformed to ritual,
whose rhythm conformed to music,
and who hit the target more often
were allowed to participate in sacrifices.
Those whose deportment did not conform to ritual,
whose rhythm did not conform to music,
Those of middle and young age
are not allowed to participate in the sacrifices.
If they frequently participate in the sacrifices, the ruler will have celebrations;
if they infrequently participate in the sacrifices, the ruler will have reprimands.
Frequent celebrations lead to increased territory;
frequent reprimands lead to decreased territory.
Therefore, it is said:
"Shooting
is for the feudal lords."
Therefore, the feudal lords and their ministers devote themselves to shooting
in order to practice ritual and music.
A ruler and his ministers practicing ritual and music yet still leading to ruin and exile
has never happened.
47.6 Therefore, the *Classic of Poetry* says:
"The descendant, the Hóu clan,
the four directions are all provided for;
great officers and gentlemen,
together with the common scholars,
whether small or great, none are out of place,
they attend the lord's place,
for banquets and for archery,
then there are banquets and praise."
It says that the ruler and his ministers together devote themselves to archery
in order to practice ritual and music,
then there will be peace and praise.
Therefore, the Son of Heaven established it,
and the feudal lords strive for it.
This is how the Son of Heaven nourishes the feudal lords,
And arms are not used,
the lords are creating their own means of governance.
47.7 Kǒngzǐ shot arrows at the Jué Xiāng hunting ground,
the spectators were like a wall.
When the shooting reached the Sīmǎ,
he made Zǐlù hold the bow and arrows,
go out and announce the shooting, saying:
"Generals who flee from the army,
grand masters of destroyed states,
and those who are in subservient positions will not enter,
the rest may enter."
Approximately half left,
half entered.
Then he made Gōng Wǎng zhī Qiú and Xù Diǎn
raise their cups and speak:
Gōng Wǎng zhī Qiú raised his cup and said:
"The young and strong are filial and fraternal,
the elderly love ritual,
do not follow vulgar customs,
cultivate themselves while awaiting death,
don't they?
They are in this position."
Approximately half left,
half remained.
Xù Diǎn then raised his cup and said:
"Those who love learning and are never tired of it,
love ritual and never change,
the aged and those in mourning who can speak correctly without confusion,
No?
One is in this position."
Indeed, the custom still exists.
47.8 "Shooting" as a word means "to elaborate,"
some say "to release."
"To elaborate" means
each elaborates upon his own will.
Therefore, with a calm mind and upright posture,
holding the bow and arrow carefully and firmly,
holding the bow and arrow carefully and firmly,
then one will hit the target.
Therefore it is said:
"He who acts as a father,
takes the father's target;
he who acts as a son,
takes the son's target;
he who acts as a ruler,
takes the ruler's target;
he who acts as a subject,
takes the subject's target."
Therefore, archers each shoot at their own target.
Therefore, the Son of Heaven's great archery
is called shooting at the *hóu*;
shooting at the *hóu*
means shooting to become a feudal lord (*zhūhóu*).
If one shoots and hits, then one may become a feudal lord;
if one shoots and does not hit, then one may not become a feudal lord.
47.9 When the Son of Heaven is about to perform a sacrifice,
One must first practice archery in the marsh.
A marsh
is the place for selecting gentlemen.
After having shot in the marsh,
then one shoots in the archery hall.
Those who hit the target are allowed to participate in the sacrifice;
those who do not hit the target are not allowed to participate in the sacrifice.
Those who are not allowed to participate in the sacrifice are admonished,
and their land is reduced;
those who are allowed to participate in the sacrifice are congratulated,
and their land is increased.
Advancing rank and diminishing land is the way.
47.10 Therefore, when a boy is born,
a mulberry bow and reed arrows, six of them,
are used to shoot at heaven and earth and the four directions.
Heaven and earth and the four directions
are what a man is responsible for.
Therefore, one must first have aspirations for what one is responsible for,
and only then dare to use grain.
This refers to eating food.
47.11 Archery
is the way of benevolence.
Archery seeks correctness within oneself;
only after oneself is correct does one release the arrow;
if the arrow is released and does not hit the target,
then one does not resent those who have won over oneself,
but instead seeks the cause within oneself.
Confucius (Kǒngzǐ) said:
"The junzi has nothing to contend for;
if he must contend, it is in archery!
Bowing and yielding they ascend,
descending they drink;
their contention is that of a junzi."
47.12 Kǒngzǐ said:
"How does an archer shoot? How does he listen?
Following the sound and releasing [the arrow],
releasing it without missing the target,
that is surely the mark of a worthy person!
As for the unworthy,
how could they possibly hit the mark?"
The *Shī* (Book of Poetry) says:
"Release those arrows that hit the mark,
in order to seek your rank."
*Qí* (祈)
means to seek;
seeking to hit the mark in order to decline rank.
Wine
is for nourishing the elderly,
and for nourishing the sick;
seeking to hit the mark in order to decline rank
is declining nourishment.
*Yàn Yì* (燕義)
48.1 In ancient times, the Zhōu (周) Son of Heaven's (周天子) court
had the office of *shùzǐ* (庶子).
The *shùzǐ* office oversaw the *shùzǐ* of the feudal lords,
When the common sons of the *qīng* 卿 (ministers), *dàfū* 大夫 (high officials), and
*shì* 士 (lower officials) die,
he is in charge of their cautionary instructions [regarding the funeral rites],
and directs their instruction and governance [of the household affairs],
differentiating their ranks,
and correcting their positions.
When the state has major affairs,
he then leads the state sons and presents them to the heir apparent,
to be used as he sees fit.
If there are matters of armored warfare,
he then provides them with chariots and armor,
aligns their troops and companies,
establishes their officers,
and governs them with military law,
which the *Sīmǎ* 司馬 (Minister of War) does not correct.
In all the political affairs of the state,
the state sons are kept for travel and service,
and are made to cultivate virtue and study the Way,
in the spring, they are assembled for the schools,
in the autumn, they are assembled for archery,
in order to examine their skills and promote or demote them.
48.2 The Significance of the Feasting Ritual of the Lords:
The lord stands southeast of the eastern steps,
facing south to greet the *qīng* 卿 and
*dàfū* 大夫 (high officials), who all advance a little,
to take their positions;
the lord sits on the steps to the east,
residing in the principal position;
The ruler alone ascends and stands on the mat,
facing west and standing distinctly.
This signifies that none dare approach him casually.
48.3 Establishing the host and guest
is the proper etiquette for drinking wine.
Having the steward act as the presenter to the host
signifies that no subject dares to treat the ruler with equal courtesy.
Not using dukes and ministers as guests,
but using senior officials as guests,
is to avoid suspicion,
clarifying the principle of avoiding suspicion.
When the guest enters the middle of the courtyard,
the ruler descends one step and bows to him,
showing him respect.
48.4 When the ruler proposes a toast to the guest,
and when the ruler bestows a rank,
the guest descends, bows twice, and kowtows,
then ascends and completes the bow,
clarifying the etiquette of a subject.
The ruler returns the bow,
because etiquette requires that every bow be returned,
clarifying the etiquette of the ruler above.
When subjects exert their strength and exhaust their abilities to establish merit for the state,
the ruler must reward them with titles and emoluments.
Therefore, all subjects strive to exert their strength and exhaust their abilities to establish merit.
Thus, the state is secure and the ruler is at peace.
"Etiquette requires that every bow be returned"
means that the ruler does not take from his subjects without giving back.
The ruler must understand and clarify the correct path to guide the people.
When the people are guided by this path and achieve results,
only then should he take one-tenth of their produce.
Therefore, the ruler has sufficient resources, and the people are not impoverished.
This is why those above and those below are harmonious and do not resent each other.
Harmony and peace
are the purpose of ritual.
This is the great principle between ruler and subject, those above and those below.
Therefore, it is said:
"The *yàn lǐ* banquet ritual
is that by which the meaning of the relationship between ruler and subject is clarified."
48.5 Seating:
*Xiǎo qīng* are seated next to *shàng qīng*,
*dàfū* are seated next to *xiǎo qīng*,
*shì* and commoners are seated in order below.
Presenting to the ruler,
the ruler raises his cup and offers a return toast.
Afterwards, presenting to the *qīng*,
the *qīng* raises his cup and offers a return toast.
Afterwards, presenting to the *dàfū*,
the *dàfū* raises his cup and offers a return toast.
Afterwards, presenting to the *shì*,
the *shì* raises his cup and offers a return toast.
Afterwards, presenting to the commoners.
The sacrificial stands, dishes, sacrificial animals, offerings, and delicacies
all have different grades,
by which nobility and commonness are made clear.
The Meaning of Engagement
49.1 The betrothal gifts,
for a Duke, consist of seven go-betweens;
for a Marquis or Earl, five go-betweens;
for a Viscount or Baron, three go-betweens.
This is to clarify the distinctions of rank.
The go-between relays the message,
and the gentleman does not dare to question his superior,
this is the utmost respect.
49.2 He yields three times before relaying the message,
yields three times before entering the temple gate,
makes three bows before reaching the steps,
yields three times before ascending,
this is to express respect and deference.
49.3 The ruler sends a *shì* to greet at the border,
a *dàfū* offers suburban hospitality,
the ruler personally greets him with bows inside the great gate and receives him in the temple,
facing north to acknowledge the gift,
bowing in acknowledgment of the honor of the ruler's command,
this is to show utmost respect.
49.4 Respect and deference,
are the means by which gentlemen interact.
Therefore, if the feudal lords interact with respect and deference,
they will not encroach upon each other.
49.5 A *qīng* serves as the senior presenter,
a *dàfū* serves as the assistant presenter,
and a *shì* serves as the successor presenter.
The ruler personally shows courtesy to the guest,
Private meetings with guests,
private audiences,
sending cooked food and grain,
returning *gui* and *zhang* jade objects,
providing bribes and gifts,
banquets, meals, and feasts,
these are the means to clarify the proper relationship between guests, ministers, and the ruler.
49.6 Therefore, the Son of Heaven controlled the feudal lords
by having them conduct minor audiences every year,
and major audiences every three years,
encouraging each other with ritual.
If an envoy made a mistake during an audience,
the host ruler would not personally offer him a meal.
This was a way to shame and encourage them.
If the feudal lords encouraged each other with ritual,
then outwardly they would not invade each other,
and inwardly they would not violate each other.
This is how the Son of Heaven supported the feudal lords.
Soldiers would not be needed
and the feudal lords would naturally rectify themselves.
49.7 Using *gui* and *zhang* jade objects as gifts,
is to emphasize ritual;
once the audience is over, returning the *gui* and *zhang*,
this embodies the principle of valuing ritual over wealth.
If the feudal lords encouraged each other to value ritual over wealth,
then the people would develop a custom of yielding.
49.8 The host country treats guests
with three layers of provision for entrance and exit;
To provide food to guests in the house,
the implements for the *wǔ láo* (five sacrificial animals) are displayed inside,
thirty cartloads of rice,
thirty cartloads of grain,
hay and firewood double the grain,
all displayed outside,
five pairs of fowl are presented daily,
all the retainers have sacrificial animals provided for them,
one meal, then another offering,
banquets and timely gifts are countless;
this is how one enriches and values ritual.
49.9 Those in ancient times who used wealth could not all do it equally well,
but the reason why the use of wealth was so generous
is that words were exhausted in the performance of ritual.
Exhausting oneself in the performance of ritual
means that internally ruler and ministers do not encroach upon each other,
and externally they do not invade each other.
Therefore, the Son of Heaven regulates it,
and the feudal lords are committed to it.
49.10 The rituals of betrothal and archery
are the most important rituals.
One begins the affairs at dawn,
and the ritual is completed only when the sun is almost at its zenith.
Those who are not strong and capable cannot perform them.
Therefore, those who are strong and capable
will use this to perform the rituals.
The wine is clear,
but people are thirsty and dare not drink it;
Dried meat;
People are hungry but dare not eat it;
The sun sets, and people are weary,
Qí Zhuāng,
are correct and reverent
and dare not slack off.
In order to complete rituals and customs,
in order to correct the relationship between ruler and minister,
in order to make close the relationship between father and son,
in order to harmonize elders and juniors.
This is what is difficult for most people,
but the gentleman practices it,
therefore it is called having conduct;
having conduct is called having righteousness,
having righteousness is called bravery.
Therefore, what is valued in bravery,
is valued in its ability to establish righteousness;
what is valued in establishing righteousness,
is valued in having conduct;
what is valued in having conduct,
is valued in practicing rituals.
Therefore, what is valued in bravery,
is valued in daring to practice rituals and righteousness.
Therefore, bravery, strength, and power,
when the world is at peace,
are used in rituals and righteousness;
when the world is in turmoil,
are used in victory in battle.
Using it in warfare, one will be invincible;
using it in rites and righteousness, one will govern smoothly;
outwardly invincible,
inwardly governed smoothly,
this is called flourishing virtue.
Therefore, the sage-kings valued courage and strength
in this way.
If courage and strength
are not used in rites and righteousness or to achieve victory in war,
but are used in fighting and contention,
then one is called a rebellious person.
When punishments are carried out in the state,
those executed are rebellious people.
If this is the case,
then the people will be governed smoothly and the state will be secure.
49.11 Zǐ Gòng 子貢 asked Confucius Kǒngzǐ 孔子, saying:
"May I ask why the superior man values jade and despises pebbles?
Is it because jade is scarce and pebbles are plentiful?"
Confucius Kǒngzǐ 孔子 said:
"It is not because pebbles are plentiful
that they are despised,
but because jade is scarce
that it is valued.
In the past, the superior man compared virtues to jade.
Warm and lustrous,
this is rén 仁 (benevolence);
dense and firm,
this is zhì 智 (wisdom);
To be upright but not cutting,
that is righteousness;
to hang down like a falling object,
that is ritual;
to strike it and its sound is clear, high-pitched, and long,
its ending abruptly stopping,
that is music;
a flaw not concealing the jade, and the jade not concealing the flaw,
that is loyalty;
trustworthiness reaching far and wide,
that is trustworthiness;
the breath like a white rainbow,
that is Heaven;
the spirit appearing in mountains and rivers,
that is Earth;
the *guī* and *zhāng* pendants uniquely reaching understanding,
that is virtue.
What all under Heaven value,
that is the Way.
The *Book of Odes* says:
"When I think of the noble person,
his warmth is like jade."
Therefore, noble persons value it."
The Four Regulations of Mourning Garments
50.1 Generally, the grand system of ritual
embodies Heaven and Earth,
models the four seasons,
Zé yīnyáng, [Analyze yin and yang,]
shùn rénqíng, [conform to human feelings,]
gù wèi zhī lǐ. [therefore it is called ritual.]
Zī zhī zhě, [Those who criticize it,]
shì bùzhī lǐ zhī suǒ yóu shēng yě. [do not understand how ritual arises.]
50.2 Fú lǐ, [Indeed, ritual,]
jíxiōng yì dào, [good fortune and misfortune are different paths,]
bùdé xiānggān, [they must not interfere with each other,]
qǔ zhī yīnyáng yě. [this is derived from yin and yang.]
Sàng yǒu sì zhì, [Mourning has four regulations,]
biàn ér cóngyí, [they change and follow what is appropriate,]
qǔ zhī sìshí yě. [this is derived from the four seasons.]
Yǒu ēn yǒu lǐ, [There is kindness and principle,]
yǒu jié yǒu quán, [there is moderation and expediency,]
qǔ zhī rénqíng yě. [this is derived from human feelings.]
Ēn zhě rén yě, [Kindness is benevolence,]
lǐ zhě yì yě, [principle is righteousness,]
jié zhě lǐ yě, [moderation is ritual,]
quán zhě zhì yě. [expediency is wisdom.]
Rényì lǐ zhì, [Benevolence, righteousness, ritual, and wisdom,]
rén dào jù yǐ. [the principles of humanity are complete.]
50.3 Qí ēn hòu zhě, [Those whose kindness is deep,]
qí fú zhòng; [their mourning garments are heavy;]
gù wèi fù zhǎncuī sān nián, [therefore, for a father, one wears the roughest mourning for three years,]
yǐ ēn zhì zhě yě. [this is regulated by kindness.]
50.4 Mén nèi zhī zhì, [The management within the household,]
ēn yǎn yì; [kindness overshadows righteousness;]
mén wài zhī zhì, [the management outside the household,]
Severing Righteousness from Favor.
Serving one's ruler with the same resources as serving one's father
results in equal respect.
Honoring the honorable and respecting the respectable
are the greatest forms of righteousness.
Therefore, mourning for the ruler also involves the *zhǎncuī* garment for three years,
as it is controlled by righteousness.
50.5 Eating after three days,
bathing after three months,
and wearing the *liàn* garment after a year
involves diminishing, but not destroying, one's nature,
and not harming life with death.
Mourning does not exceed three years;
patching the hemp *cūshuāi* garment is forbidden,
and tombs are not enlarged;
on the day of the *xiáng* sacrifice,
a plain zither is played,
announcing to the people that there is an end;
this is controlled by moderation.
Serving one's mother with the same resources as serving one's father
results in equal love.
Heaven has no two suns,
the earth has no two kings,
a state has no two rulers,
a family has no two superiors;
it is governed by one.
Therefore, while the father is alive,
wearing the hemmed *qícuī* garment for a year for the mother
見無二尊也。
50.6 What is the staff for?
It is a jué (爵, rank).
On the third day, a son is given a staff;
on the fifth day, a dàfū (大夫, high-ranking official) is given a staff;
on the seventh day, a shì (士, scholar-official) is given a staff.
Some say it "supports the master";
some say it "aids the infirm,"
women and children do not use staffs,
because they are not capable of infirmity.
When all officials are prepared,
and all things are ready,
and affairs are carried out without instruction,
then one is aided to rise;
when affairs are carried out only after instruction,
then one is supported to rise by a staff;
when one personally attends to affairs before they are carried out,
then one's face is merely dirty.
A bald man does not do a zhuā (髽, hair bun);
a hunchback does not bare his shoulder;
a lame man does not leap;
the old and sick do not stop drinking wine and eating meat.
All these eight things
are regulated by discretionary authority.
50.7 When death has just occurred,
one should not be lax for three days,
one should not relax for three months,
one should grieve for one year,
Three years of mourning;
it is a cutting back of affection.
The sages, taking this cutting back, established a regulation,
and this is the reason why mourning lasts for three years.
The virtuous cannot exceed it,
and the unworthy cannot fail to reach it.
This is the Doctrine of the Mean in mourning;
it is what kings constantly practice.
The *Shū* (Book of Documents) says:
"Gāo Zōng (高宗) was in the *liàng àn* (諒闇)hut,
and for three years did not speak."
This was praised as good.
No king fails to perform this ritual.
Why is this alone praised as good?
The answer is:
Gāo Zōng (高宗) was Wǔ Dīng (武丁).
Wǔ Dīng (武丁)
was a worthy king of the Yīn (殷) dynasty.
Succeeding to the throne, he was compassionate and kind during the mourning period.
At this time,
the Yīn (殷) dynasty declined and then revived,
ritual was abandoned and then restored.
Therefore, it was praised as good.
Because it was praised as good,
it was recorded in the *Shū* (Book of Documents) and elevated.
Therefore, he was called Gāo Zōng (高宗).
In three years of mourning,
the ruler does not speak.
The *Book [of Documents]* says:
"Gāo Zōng, in the mourning hut,
did not speak for three years."

Concerning mourning inquiries
The *Commentary* says:
"There is 'from light to heavy',"
the wife of the Young Master mourning for her husband's paternal aunt.
"There is 'from heavy to light',"
mourning for the wife's parents.
"There is 'from no mourning garment to having a mourning garment',"
the wife of the Young Master mourning for the Young Master's maternal cousins.
"There is 'from having a mourning garment to no mourning garment',"
the Young Master mourning for his wife's parents.
The *Commentary* says:
"If the (real) mother is divorced,
then one wears mourning for the stepmother's relatives;
If the (real) mother dies,
then one wears mourning for the real mother's relatives."
Wearing mourning for the real mother's relatives,
then one does not wear mourning for the stepmother's relatives.
For the three-year mourning period,
once the linen is changed (after one year),
for the one-year mourning period,

For a *dà gōng* mourning period,
it is also like this.
For *xiǎo gōng*,
There is no change.

(of the mourning dress), put on a Zhì (絰, a hemp band worn on the head or waist);
after the removal,

once the Zhì is worn,

Use having a base as a standard.

For the elder and middle (young deceased),

When the lord acts as the Son of Heaven for three years,

*Jiàn Zhuàn*
38.1 Why does *zhǎn cuī* wear *jū*?
*Jū*,
is an ugly appearance;
it is used to cover the head inwardly and display it outwardly.
The appearance of *zhǎn cuī* is like *jū*,
the appearance of *zī cuī* is like *xǐ*,
the appearance of *dà gōng* is like [something that] stops,
for *xiǎo gōng* and *zī má*, a tolerable appearance is acceptable.
These are expressions of grief manifested in physical appearance.
The weeping of *zhǎn cuī*
is as if going away and not returning;
the weeping of *zī cuī*
is as if going away and returning;
the weeping of *dà gōng*
has three turns and then a lingering sound;
for *xiǎo gōng* and *zī má*,
a sorrowful appearance is acceptable.
These are expressions of grief manifested in sounds.
For *zhǎn cuī*,
one can only respond with "yes" and does not answer;
Wearing *qí shuāi* mourning garments,
one responds but does not speak;
wearing *dà gōng* garments,
one speaks but does not deliberate;
wearing *xiǎo gōng* and *zī mā* garments,
one deliberates but does not extend to music.
This is the expression of grief in speech.
Wearing *zhǎn shuāi* garments,
one does not eat for three days;
wearing *qí shuāi* garments,
one does not eat for two days;
wearing *dà gōng* garments,
one abstains from eating on the third day;
wearing *xiǎo gōng* and *zī mā* garments,
one abstains from eating twice;
if a *shì* (gentleman) assists with the encoffining,
then one abstains from eating once.
Therefore, in mourning for one's parents,
after the encoffinment (*bìn*), one eats congee;
in the morning, one adds a handful of rice,
and in the evening, one adds a handful of rice.
In *qí shuāi* mourning,
one eats coarse food and drinks water,
not eating vegetables or fruits.
In *dà gōng* mourning,
one does not eat vinegar or sauces.
In *xiǎo gōng* and *zī mā* mourning,
one does not drink sweet wine (*lǐ jiǔ*).
This is the expression of grief manifested in food and drink.
During the mourning period for one's parents,
after the *yú* 虞 sacrifice and the end of the weeping ceremony (*zú kū* 卒哭),
one eats coarse food and drinks water,
not eating vegetables or fruits.
After one year, at the Lesser Auspicious Sacrifice (*xiǎo xiáng* 小祥),
one eats vegetables and fruits.
After another year, at the Greater Auspicious Sacrifice (*dà xiáng* 大祥),
one has vinegar and sauce.
In the middle of the month, at the *dàn* 禫 sacrifice,
after the *dàn* 禫 sacrifice, one drinks sweet wine (*lǐ jiǔ* 醴酒).
Those who begin drinking wine first drink sweet wine.
Those who begin eating meat first eat dried meat.
During the mourning period for one's parents,
one dwells in a lean-to (*yǐ lú* 倚廬),
sleeping on straw and using a clod of earth as a pillow,
not removing the hemp headband and belt.
During the *qí cuī* 齊衰 mourning period,
one dwells in a whitewashed room (*è shì* 堊室),
without using rush mats (*hù jiǎn* 芐翦).
During the *dà gōng* 大功 mourning period,
one sleeps with a mat.
For *xiǎo gōng* 小功 and *zī má* 緦麻 mourning,
a bed is acceptable.
This is the expression of grief manifested in dwelling.
During the mourning period for one's parents,
after the *yú* 虞 sacrifice and the end of the weeping ceremony (*zú kū* 卒哭),
the pillars and beams are trimmed, and screens are set up,
Hù Jiǎn did not accept.
After one year, the Xiǎo Xiáng sacrifice was performed;
one lived in a whitewashed room,
and slept with a mat.
After another year, the Dà Xiáng sacrifice was performed;
one lived in the original sleeping quarters.
In the middle of the month, the Dàn sacrifice was performed,
and after the Dàn sacrifice, one slept on a bed.
For Zhǎncuī mourning, three *shēng* (升) of cloth were used;
for Qícuī mourning, four, five, or six *shēng* were used;
for Dàgōng mourning, seven, eight, or nine *shēng* were used;
for Xiǎogōng mourning, ten, eleven, or twelve *shēng* were used;
for Zīmá mourning, fifteen *shēng* were used, with half removed.
If there were duties, the cloth was woven fine; if not, it was plain cloth, called Zī.
These are the expressions of grief in clothing.
For Zhǎncuī mourning, three *shēng* were used.
After the Jìyú and Zúcū sacrifices,
one received six *shēng* of finished cloth and a seven *shēng* hat;
for mourning for one's mother with Shūcuī, four *shēng* were used,
and one received seven *shēng* of finished cloth and an eight *shēng* hat.
Linen clothing was replaced with kudzu clothing,
and the kudzu belt was worn in three layers.
After one year, the Xiǎo Xiáng sacrifice was performed;
one wore a linen hat with a crimson edge,
but the waist band was not removed.
Men removed the head covering,
women removed the belt.
Why did men remove the head covering?
Why does a woman remove her sash during mourning?
Men value headwear,
women value sashes.
When removing mourning garments, one starts with what is valued most.
When changing garments, one starts with what is less important.
After one year comes the Great Auspicious Sacrifice (dàxiáng),
with plain white silk (sù gǎo) and hemp clothing (má yī).
In the middle of the month comes the Dàn Sacrifice,
after the Dàn Sacrifice, finer cloth is used,
and one wears all the usual accessories.
Why change garments?
Because one starts with what is less important.
In a mourning period for Zhǎncuī,
after the Jìyú and Zúcū ceremonies,
if one encounters a mourning period for Qícuī,
the less important garment is used to wrap,
the more important garment is worn separately.
After the Liàn Sacrifice,
if one encounters a mourning period for Dàgōng,
hemp (má) and kudzu (gě) are worn doubly.
38.2 In a mourning period for Qícuī,
after the Jìyú and Zúcū ceremonies,
if one encounters a mourning period for Dàgōng,
hemp (má) and kudzu (gě) are worn together.
38.3 Kudzu (gě) for Zhǎncuī,
is the same as hemp (má) for Qícuī;
kudzu (gě) for Qícuī,
is the same as hemp (má) for Dàgōng;
The coarse hemp cloth (gé) for Dàgōng
is the same as the fine hemp cloth (má) for Xiǎogōng;
the coarse hemp cloth (gé) for Xiǎogōng
is the same as the fine hemp cloth (má) for Zī má.
If the hemp cloths are the same, then one wears both.
When wearing both, the heavier mourning

Question about the three-year mourning
39.1 What is the significance of the three-year mourning?
The Master said:
"It establishes rules based on emotions,
and thus regulates the community,
distinguishing the degrees of closeness, nobility, and humbleness,
which cannot be increased or decreased.
Therefore, it is said:
'There is no changing this principle.'"
The greater the wound, the longer it takes to heal;
the deeper the pain, the slower it is to subside.
The three-year mourning
establishes rules based on emotions,
and is the extreme expression of the deepest sorrow.
Unhemmed mourning clothes (zhǎncuī), a staff of coarse straw (zūzhàng),
living in a thatched hut (yǐlú),
eating porridge,
sleeping on straw and using a clod of earth as a pillow (chānzhěnkuài),
are the ways of expressing the extreme pain.
The three-year mourning
Completed in twenty-five months.
Grief and pain not yet exhausted,
longing and remembrance not yet forgotten,
yet mourning is ended in this way.
Is it not that seeing off the dead has its limit,
and returning to life has its boundaries?
39.2 Generally, those who live between Heaven and Earth,
creatures with blood and breath,
must have knowledge;
those with knowledge,
none do not know to love their own kind.
Now, even large birds and beasts,
upon losing their mates,
after months and seasons have passed,
will surely return and patrol,
passing their old home,
circling and hovering there,
crying and calling out,
stamping and pacing,
hesitating and lingering,
and only then are they able to leave.
The smallest, even sparrows,
still chirp and twitter for a while,
and only then are they able to leave.
Therefore, among creatures with blood and breath,
none is more knowledgeable than humans;
thus, a person's feelings for their parents
never cease until death.
39.3 If one were to follow a person suffering from evil lewdness,
they would forget it by evening what they died for in the morning.
Yet to follow them
would be worse than birds and beasts.
How could they live together in a group without causing chaos?
39.4 If one were to follow a gentleman of refined cultivation,
the three-year mourning period
would end in twenty-five months,
like a team of horses passing a crack.
Yet to continue it
would be endless.
39.5 Therefore, the former kings established central regulations and limitations for it,
using them just once to form patterns and principles,
and then released them.
39.6 Then how is the one-year period arrived at?
It is said:
It is determined by the one-year period for the closest relatives.
Why is this?
It is said:
The heavens and earth have already changed,
the four seasons have already transformed,
and everything within the heavens and earth
is beginning anew.
It is symbolized by this.
39.7 Then why is it three years?
It is said:
It is to add to the importance of it.
How to make it double?
Therefore, it is called "Zài Qī" (再期, another year).
39.8 Why does it start from the ninth month and below?
It is said:
How could one allow it to be insufficient?
Therefore, three years is considered the most solemn,
"zī má" (緦麻) and "xiǎo gōng" (小功) are considered diminished,
"Qī" (期, one year) and nine months are considered intermediate.
Above, it takes its image from Heaven;
below, it takes its model from Earth;
in the middle, it takes its principle from Man.
The reasons why people live together in harmony and unity are all contained within.
Therefore, the three-year mourning period
is the most refined expression of human conduct,
and this is what is called the utmost solemnity.
It is what all kings of the past agreed upon,
what is unified from ancient times to the present.
There has been no one who knew from where it originated.
Kǒngzǐ (孔子) said:
"A child is three years old
before being weaned from the embrace of his parents;
therefore, the three-year mourning period
is the universal mourning period under Heaven."
Shēn Yī (深衣, Deep Robe)
In ancient times, the "Shēn Yī" (深衣, Deep Robe)
certainly had standards
to conform to the compass, square, line, weight, and balance.
It should not be so short as to expose the skin,
Do not let the hem drag in the dirt.
Continue the lapel,
hook the edges.
The waist seam should be half an inch down;
The height of the armhole
should allow for elbow movement;
The length of the sleeves
should be such that when bent back, they reach the elbow.
The belt below should not press on the hip,
above should not press on the ribs,
where there are no bones.
Specifications:
Twelve widths of fabric to correspond to the twelve months;
The sleeves are round to correspond to the compass;
The curved collar is like a square to correspond to the square;
The back seam reaches the ankle to correspond to the straight;
The hem is even like the balance to correspond to the level.
Therefore, the compass
represents proper conduct and raising one's hand with decorum;
carrying the plumb line and embracing the square
is to straighten one's governance,
and to square one's righteousness.
Therefore, the *Yì* says:
"The movement of 'Kun' (Earth) in the second line,
is straight by means of the square."
The hem being even like the balance
is to settle the will and calm the heart.
These five principles having been applied,
therefore the sages wore them.
Therefore, the compass and square are valued for their impartiality,
the plumb line is valued for its straightness,
the balance is valued for its evenness,
therefore the former kings esteemed them.
